h: פָּרָשַׁת שְׁקָלִים, מַאֲמָר ב׳ Parshas Shekalim — Maamar Bais

p: "On the first of Adar they announce concerning the shekalim,
etc." And we read it on the first of Adar
so that they should bring shekalim to the Mikdash.
From the Gemara's wording it would appear
that what we learned, "they announce concerning the shekalim,"
means through the reading of the parshah,
and although they read it earlier, on the Shabbos
when it falls in the middle of the week,
the first of Adar is merely the latest time.
"they announce" means by proclamation of the beis din,
throughout all of Israel and proclaims;
and likewise the Rambam, in Hilchos Shekalim
brought the law that they announce concerning the shekalim,
he brought the law of reading Parshas Shekalim.
It is clear that these are two separate matters,
and we must understand the reason for reading the parshah.
And if we say that nowadays,
when there are no shekalim and no Mikdash,
in the same way that we read the sections of the korbanos,
on account of "And we will render for bulls the offering of our lips,"
then what they said in the Gemara cannot be understood:
"And we read it on the first of Adar
so that they should bring shekalim to the Mikdash,"
which states explicitly that the enactment of reading the parshah
was in force even at the time
when the Beis HaMikdash was standing.
So why did they read it then?
Surely they would send out messengers
on the first of Adar to proclaim it!
But the explanation is based on
וּפָרָשִׁיּוֹת שֶׁקּוֹרִין בָּהֶם בְּכָל שַׁבָּת וְכוּלֵּי
and the parshiyos that are read each Shabbos, etc.,
And at Parshas Shekalim Moshe said:
once I die, I am no longer mentioned!'
אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא חַיֶּיךָ
The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: 'By your life,
that they read it before Me,
it is as if you stand there
and lift up their heads,' etc."
And it has already been asked
why did Moshe not sense this
regarding the sections of the korbanos,
only while the Beis HaMikdash stands?
And as for the answer given from the sefer Gevul Binyamin
for Parshas Vayakhel and Shekalim, p. 104),
that he has an awesome premise:
בְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ בִּזְמַן הַזֶּה גַּם כֵּן
in the Beis HaMikdash even nowadays,
that were hidden away for this, etc.,
and therefore he did not sense anything
regarding the sections of the korbanos, which apply forever,
which is not so with shekalim,
which lapse after the Churban, etc.;
there is the parshah of the anointing oil,
שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה רַק מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה מֹשֶׁה
of which there was only what Moshe made,
and that endures for the future,
and the anointing oil was hidden away
at the end of the First Temple
and likewise there are several parshiyos
שֶׁלֹּא נָהֲגוּ רַק לִשְׁעָתָם בְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹר
that applied only for their time, in that generation,
so why did he not ask about them?
And in truth, as for what they explain
(see Etz Yosef on the Tanchuma, ibid.),
that he sensed regarding Parshas Shekalim
that it would lapse after the Churban—
"once I die, I am no longer mentioned,"
מַשְׁמַע שֶׁשָּׁאַל עַל אַחַר פְּטִירָתוֹ תֵּיכֶף
it implies that he asked about the time right after his passing,
and then there was still to come the Mishkan of Shiloh,
and the Eternal House, and the Second Temple—
that he certainly did not ask
about any parshah that is no longer in practice,
since in any case the reading of it is
"And we will render for bulls the offering of our lips,"
and his lips move in the grave
Rather, his question concerned Parshas Shekalim,
for it is brought in Pesikta Rabbasi
"When Moshe came down to meet Israel
and they saw that excellent and praiseworthy thing"—
that is, the rays of glory, etc.—
They said: We are in decline, etc.,
and you too, Moshe, were with us,
before the Holy One, blessed be He, etc.
The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him:
Go, raise up their heads, etc.;
אַף אֲנִי אֶזְקוֹף רֹאשָׁם שֶׁל בָּנַי
I too will lift up the heads of My children:
That is: just as Moshe Rabbeinu restores
as written in Pri Etz Chaim
so too with shekalim: when they give the shekalim,
even though it is on a weekday,
Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him,
וְאָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ זוֹקֵף אֶת רֹאשָׁם
and then Hashem lifts up their heads
And one may explain that this is what they said
אָמַר מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
"Moshe said before the Holy One, blessed be He:
'Through what will the horn of Israel be raised?'
He said to him: 'Through "When you lift up."'"
"take from them a ransom for charity,"
מִכָּל מָקוֹם פְּשָׁטֵיהּ קָאֵי עַל הַשְּׁקָלִים
nevertheless its plain sense refers to the shekalim,
and "the horn of Israel will be raised"
indicates up to the very heights,
for so the term "ram," exalted, indicates
beyond the grasp of human beings.
which came to atone for the sin of the Golden Calf—
as they said in the Midrash
and so it is in the Yerushalmi
(שְׁקָלִים פֶּרֶק ב הֲלָכָה ג ט, ב)
and at the sin of the Calf they stripped off the crowns
and Moshe merited and took them,
and since the sin was rectified
מַחֲזִיר לָהֶם מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, restores to them
the crowns even on a weekday,
and thereby he raises the horn of Israel
Therefore he asked at Parshas Shekalim:
since the raising of Israel's horn
even though the Beis HaMikdash would still stand
nevertheless he would not be mentioned,
and through what would the horn of Israel be raised?
For he thought that there would cease
the raising of the horn by restoring the crowns.
that at the time of the reading of Parshas Shekalim
כְּאִלּוּ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם עוֹמֵד
as if Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, were standing
And when they read the section of Shekalim
on its own Shabbos, in Parshas Ki Sisa,
הוּא קְרִיאָה כְּכָל קְרִיאַת פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת הַתּוֹרָה
it is a reading like any reading of the Torah's parshiyos;
only when they read the parshah
or on the first of Adar
אָז מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ זוֹקֵף אֶת רֹאשָׁם
does Moshe Rabbeinu then lift up their heads.
For the Torah is called the Torah of Moshe,
since he encompassed all the souls
which are the letters of the Torah;
and when they read the parshah,
its letters, which are the soul
of Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him—
it is as if Moshe were standing
and lifting up their heads then,
and restoring the crowns to them.
but the reading of the parshah
or on the first of Adar benefits Israel,
so that when they bring the shekalim afterward on a weekday,
אָז גַּם כֵּן יוּחְזַר לָהֶם הַכְּתָרִים
then too the crowns will be restored to them,
just as he used to restore them
at the time they gave their shekalim
וְהָיָה זוֹקֵף אֶת רֹאשָׁם כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
and he would lift up their heads, as mentioned above.
cited in the sefer Gevul Binyamin
הִיא מֵהָרַב מְנַחֵם עֲזַרְיָה זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה
comes from the Rema MiPano, of blessed memory
and we do not know its source.
granted, the korbanos that Eliyahu offers
from the lambs that he buys
but the shekalim hidden away for this purpose
from the time of the Beis HaMikdash—
how will they benefit that generation,
since they did not give shekalim?
"and the mussaf of this such-and-such day
even though there is no Mikdash
and it is impossible to offer it on its day;
but since the will and the longing are there
to fulfill it and to offer it,
this longing counts as the deed,
along the lines of what they said (Kiddushin 40a):
"If a person intended to do a mitzvah
and was prevented and did not do it,
as if he had done it."
And especially when one recites the verses of the korbanos,
"And we will render for bulls the offering of our lips,"
and the movement of one's mouth constitutes a deed,
and it is as if it were done.
So too with the reading of Parshas Shekalim:
has a longing and a will
to fulfill it in actual practice,
and if there were a Mikdash,
so that his shekel would reach Yerushalayim;
from this longing actual shekalim are made.
regarding Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who said,
and it began to pour forth golden dinars before them;
כָּל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יָכוֹל לַעֲשׂוֹת
All the more so can Hashem make something
out of Israel's longing and their will
to fulfill the mitzvah of shekalim,
and He makes from it actual shekalim,
and a valley fills up with shekalim,
just as they did in the time of the Beis HaMikdash,
and buys korbanos with them and offers them,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַב מְנַחֵם עֲזַרְיָה זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה
as the Rema MiPano, of blessed memory, wrote;
and so shekalim are in effect even nowadays.
On the contrary, the longing nowadays
יוֹתֵר מִמַּה שֶּׁהָיָה בִּזְמַן הַבַּיִת כַּנּוֹדָע
is greater than it was in the time of the Beis HaMikdash, as is known,
and from the longing actual shekalim are made,
and from them come the korbanos.
וְעַל זֶה מוֹעִיל קְרִיאַת הַפָּרָשָׁה דִּשְׁקָלִים
And for this the reading of Parshas Shekalim is effective
so that when the shekalim come on Rosh Chodesh Nissan,
if it falls on a weekday—
and even if it falls on Shabbos,
surely Eliyahu buys the korbanos on a weekday—
the reading of the parshah will then be effective
כְּאִלּוּ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם עוֹמֵד
as if Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, were standing
that is, that the crowns will be restored to them
for on Shabbos, even without this,
Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him,
as cited above from Pri Etz Chaim.
And this is what the Gemara says:
we go ahead and read it on the first of Adar
so that they should bring shekalim to the Mikdash";
meaning that even nowadays it is effective,
so that shekalim are made from the longing
and Eliyahu will separate terumah from them
to offer from the new terumah;
וְעַל יְדֵי קְרִיאַת הַפָּרָשָׁה מוֹעִיל זֶה
and through the reading of the parshah this is effective,
כְּאִלּוּ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם עוֹמֵד
as if Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, were standing
That is: the letters of the Torah,
which are the soul of Moshe—
it is as if he stands and lifts up their heads,
so that when they give the shekalim
the horn of Israel will be raised,
and the blemish of the Calf will be repaired,
on account of which they stripped the crowns from Israel;
Moshe Rabbeinu will restore the crowns to them.
And the reading was instituted on Shabbos,
which is the gift of the portion
of Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him,
and he restores the crowns then;
and the Shabbos of Parshas Shekalim is effective
so that the crowns are restored to Israel even on a weekday,
from the will and longing of Israel, as mentioned above.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 29b — “Rabbi Tavi said in the name of Rabbi Yoshiyya: Scripture says, ‘This is the burnt offering of the month in its month.’ The Torah said: Renew the offerings and bring them from a new contribution. Since in Nisan they must bring offerings from a new contribution, we precede it and read on the first of Adar, so that they will bring shekels to the Temple.” The discussion begins on 29a and continues on 29b. This sentence describes the public reading as preparation for the new sacrificial fund; Rav Tzadok asks how it relates to the separate proclamation.

paragraphs.text: Rashi, Megillah 29a, s.v. Mashmiin al hashekalim — “They make announcements concerning the shekalim: by proclamation of the court.”

rich.text: — “They make announcements concerning the shekalim: by proclamation of the court.”

paragraphs.text: Bartenura, Shekalim 1:1 — “The court sends throughout all the cities of Israel and proclaims that they should bring their shekalim. For on the first of Nisan the communal sacrifices must be brought from a new collection. ... Therefore they announce thirty days earlier, from the first of Adar, that the people should bring their shekalim.” The intervening exposition derives the new collection from the annual renewal of the offerings. The announcement is a court-administered act, distinct from the Torah reading.

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Shekalim 1:9 — “On the first of Adar they make announcements concerning the shekalim, so that each person will prepare his half-shekel and be ready to give it. On the fifteenth the money changers sit in every province and request payment gently: whoever gives to them, they accept from him; whoever has not given is not compelled to give.”

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Tefillah 13:20 — “When Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbos, they read the section of Shekalim and read the haftarah of Yehoyada the priest. Likewise, if Rosh Chodesh Adar falls during the week, even on Friday, they read the section of Shekalim in advance on the preceding Shabbos.” The Rambam codifies the reading among the laws of public prayer, separately from the proclamation and collection in Hilchos Shekalim. This separation is the basis of Rav Tzadok's question.

paragraphs.text: Hosea 14:3 — “Take words with you and return to Hashem. Say to Him: Forgive all iniquity and accept what is good; we shall render bulls through our lips.” The verse supplies the language by which prayer and verbal service take the place of animal offerings when they cannot be brought.

paragraphs.text: Anaf Yosef, Tanchuma, Ki Sisa §3 — “‘Master of the worlds, after I die I am not remembered.’ It is difficult: why did Moses become concerned in the section of shekels, and not in the section of offerings, since they too apply only when the Temple stands? We may answer that we have a wondrous premise: Elijah is the one who offers in the Temple. ... He has funds from the contribution of the chamber, hidden away for this purpose. Concerning this we learned, ‘I have heard that sacrifices may be offered even though there is no Temple.’ ... Therefore he did not become concerned about the section of offerings, because they are still offering them. But the section of shekels applies only when the Temple stands. He said: After I die, and the Temple is destined to be destroyed, I am not remembered. He replied: By your life! Since remembrance of the shekels remains through reading about them every year ... ‘Ki tissa’ is future tense: his name will forever be remembered in this section. (Gevul Binyamin.)” Anaf Yosef expressly cites Gevul Binyamin for this explanation. Rav Tzadok next challenges the explanation with other time-bound sections, then develops his own account of Moses restoring Israel’s crowns.

paragraphs.text: Gevul Binyamin, I, derush 54, 104a — “Elijah is the one who offers sacrifices in the Temple even in its ruined state, for the world cannot be without sacrifices. He has money from the withdrawal of the Temple treasury that was concealed for this purpose. Concerning this we learned: ‘I heard that sacrifices may be offered even though there is no Temple building’; Maimonides likewise ruled this in chapter six of the Laws of the Chosen House. The shekels, however, apply only while the Temple stands, as we learned at the end of tractate Shekalim. Moses therefore expressed no concern about the passage of the sacrifices, since they are still being offered. But concerning the passage of the shekels, which apply only while the Temple stands, he said: ‘Once I die, and the Temple is destined to be destroyed, I will not be remembered.’ God answered him: ‘By your life!’ The shekels still have a remembrance through the annual reading at that very season, on the Sabbath before the first of Adar. Thus ‘when you shall lift up’ uses the future tense: his name will always be remembered through this passage. It therefore says ‘to atone for your souls,’ since he too is included among Israel and remembered in this passage.” Gevul Binyamin states this as the premise of his homiletical explanation. His references to Mishnah Eduyos 8:6 and Maimonides concern the permissibility of sacrifices without a standing Temple building; they do not independently attest Elijah’s activity. Rav Tzaddik next questions and develops the premise.

paragraphs.text: Horayot 12a — “When the Ark was hidden away, the anointing oil was hidden away with it, together with the jar of manna, Aharon's staff with its almonds and blossoms, and the chest that the Philistines sent as a gift to the God of Israel. Who hid it away? Yoshiyahu king of Yehudah hid it away.” The preceding folio, 11b, teaches that Moshe's oil endures for the future. Its concealment by Yoshiyahu is stated on 12a; the two details should be distinguished.

paragraphs.text: Etz Yosef, Tanchuma, Ki Sisa §3 — “‘After I die I am not remembered’: for the shekels apply only while the Temple stands, as is explicitly stated at the end of tractate Shekalim. See Anaf [Yosef]. ... The future tense means that his name will forever be remembered through the reading of this section; thus the text should read.” This is the precise interpretation Rav Tzadok questions. He reads ‘after I die’ as referring to Moses’s death immediately, rather than to the later destruction of the Temple.

paragraphs.text: Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaShabbos 8 — “Every Friday night Moshe again receives the thousand portions that he lost, taking them as the additional sanctity of Shabbos. He then returns Israel's crowns to them, and from these crowns Israel inherits the additional sanctity of Shabbos each Friday. This is the meaning of Moshe rejoicing in the gift of his portion: on Shabbos the portion taken from him is given back to him as a gift, and he rejoices in what has been restored.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pekudei 9 — “Through tzedakah too one merits the light of Atika, as it says: ‘With what will Yisrael's horn be raised? With Ki Sisa’ … ‘ram’ and ‘tarum’ indicate what is beyond comprehension, the aspect of Atika.” Pekudei applies the same reading of “tarum” to tzedakah in general, so that the raising Rav Tzadok locates in Kesser is open to giving even now.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Tisa 10 — “Because they sinned at six hours, at the middle of the day, they shall give a half-shekel, which is six grammesin. Rabbi Yochanan said: Because they transgressed the Ten Commandments, each person shall therefore give ten gerah, which is a half-shekel.” The Midrash links the half-shekel with the sin of the Calf through two numerical explanations. The second also underlies the ten-gerah symbolism developed in Maamar 4.

rich.text: — “Because they sinned at six hours, at the middle of the day, they shall give a half-shekel, which is six grammesin. Rabbi Yochanan said: Because they transgressed the Ten Commandments, each person shall therefore give ten gerah, which is a half-shekel.” The Midrash links the half-shekel with the sin of the Calf through two numerical explanations. The second also underlies the ten-gerah symbolism developed in Maamar 4.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Shekalim 14 — “Because Moshe himself took the shekalim and gave them to the work of the Ohel Moed, he effected for all generations that Yisrael always act through the shekalim from the root of Moshe's level.” Maamar Yud Daled gives the reason the raising must come through Moshe: “you shall take the silver of atonement,” said to Moshe himself, made his act the channel for every later giving.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Yismach Moshe, Ki Sisa 3 — “In Mordechai's days the Temple did not stand, yet the arousal of the reading was effective … which proves that Moshe did not die and stands and serves, then as now.” The Yismach Moshe draws the same conclusion from the opposite direction: since the reading works without a Mikdash, Moshe himself is still present to lift their heads (Sotah 13b).

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Shekalim 5 — “‘We will do and offer in love according to the commandment of Your will’: through the longing to act, which is like the deed since he was prevented. It says ‘Your will,’ not ‘Your Torah.’” Maamar Hei reads the same Musaf phrase and adds the reason the longing suffices: what Hashem desires in an offering is the satisfaction of His will, and “the Holy One wants the heart.”

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 40a — “A good intention is joined to an action. ... What does for those who contemplate His name mean? Rav Assi said: Even if a person intended to perform a commandment but was prevented by circumstances and did not perform it, Scripture credits him as though he had performed it.” The source concerns credit for a sincere intention frustrated by circumstances. Rav Tzadok applies it to Israel's yearning to offer sacrifices and give shekalim when the Temple service is unavailable.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Shekalim 13 — “The Jew has no part in the korbanos except to give his shekel; the treasurers buy the offerings … so once he gave it he completed the act from his side.” Maamar Yud Gimmel answers the same difficulty, how shekalim help without an altar, by a different route: Yisrael's whole share was the giving, so the reading completes their part.
